the Nijmegan questionnaire is a good screening tool for dysfunctional breathing but is less useful in identifying patients with moderate to severely impaired quality of life who may benefit from breathing control therapy.

the Nijmegan questionnaire does not identify patients with dysfunctional breathing and breathing control therapy does not improve asthma-related quality of living.

the relationship between dysfunctional breathing (DB) and asthma and whether breathing control therapy ( BCT) can improve asthma-related quality of living in patients with moderate and severe asthma.
the identification of dysfunctional breathing (DB) and its relationship to asthma-related quality of Life (QoL) in patients attending a specialist problem asthma clinic.

there is insufficient evidence that BCT improves quality of life in asthma patients with dysfunctional breathing.
the Nijmogen questionnaire is not a useful screening tool in the assessment of dysfunctional breathing in problem asthmatics.
dysfunctional breathing is a common problem in patients with moderate or severe asthma, but the evidence for its association with asthma control is weak.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of Nijmegen Questionnaire is not an appropriate way to identify dysfunctional breathing in patients who are referred for a Problem Asthma clinic.
the Nijmegan questionnaire is a good screening tool for dysfunctional breathing but that the questionnaire is not a good tool for diagnosis of dysfunctional breathing.

we have shown that dysfunctional breathing is not uncommon in patients with moderate and severe asthma, but that a positive Njimegen questionnaire is not a reliable indicator of dysfunctional breathing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dysfunctional breathing is not a major issue in patients with moderate-severe asthma.
a positive Nijingen questionnaire does not confirm the presence of dysfunctional or inappropriate breathing in patients with problem asthma.
the Nijmegan questionnaire may be over-sensitive to dysfunctional breathing in patients presenting to a specialist asthma clinic.
